explanations.explanation: The grace of God, friend. Paul says he acted in holiness and sincerity that are from God, not in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. Look at that. The man is boasting, and the credit still goes straight to God. That's how you know it's a healthy boast.

I get why this one tempts you. Paul does sound like a confident man here. But he never points to his own strength. He says he acted in the grace of God. I run on my own strength for about one batch, and then my mustache goes limp.

Moses was Israel's leader, and his law is a big deal in the Bible. But it doesn't show up in these verses. Paul says he didn't act in worldly wisdom, but in the grace of God. So the answer is grace, and the law of Moses isn't part of this boast.

Paul says the opposite here. He writes, “we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” So no secret code, no fancy riddles. He wants them to get it, and it's a plain-letter kind of man.

That's right, friend. Paul says, “we do not write you anything that is beyond your ability to read and understand.” He's not trying to impress anybody with big mystery words. Plain and readable is the whole idea. I respect that, because my recipes have been called a lot of things, and readable is not always one of them.

Boast of each other, baker! Paul hopes they'll understand him completely, so that they may boast of him just as he will boast of them in the day of our Lord Jesus. That's a two-way street. Everybody's proud of everybody. It's a good picture of what church can look like.
I can see why a big future day makes you think of judging. But that's not what Paul writes. He hopes they'll boast of him and he'll boast of them. Nobody's holding a clipboard in this verse.

Waiting for each other sounds sweet, like holding the door at a bakery. But Paul doesn't say that here. He says he hopes the Corinthians may boast of him just as he will boast of them in the day of our Lord Jesus. Boasting is the word, so keep that one.

Double, friend! Paul planned to visit first so the Corinthians might receive a double blessing. That fits his plan to see them on the way to Macedonia and again on the way back. Double the visits, double the blessing. If a bakery gave me a double batch I'd stand on this base and cheer.

Lasting is a fine word for a blessing, but it's not the one Paul uses. He says he planned to visit first so they'd receive a double blessing. The plan had two visits in it, so double fits. Lasting just didn't make the batch.

Special sounds nice, and I'd believe it of any visit from Paul. But the word in the verse is double. He wanted them to receive a double blessing. Two stops in Corinth, one on the way in and one on the way back.

Judea it is. Paul wanted to visit Corinth on his way to Macedonia, return from Macedonia, and then have the Corinthians help him on his way to Judea. So Corinth was meant to send him off. That's a church doing some serious travel support.

Spain is a long way from this plan. These verses name Macedonia and then Judea. After returning to Corinth, Paul wanted them to help him on his way to Judea. Nobody's packing for Spain in this passage.
Galatia doesn't show up in this plan. Paul names two places: Macedonia on the way, and Judea at the end. He wanted the Corinthians to help him on his way to Judea. So that's the stop to remember.
Paul says the opposite. He swears by God's faithfulness that his message to them is not Yes and No. His word doesn't flip. When he says something about the good news, it stays said.
You got it, baker. Paul says as surely as God is faithful, his message to the Corinthians is not Yes and No. No flip-flopping on the message. The plans may change, but what he preaches stays put.

All, friend! Paul says all the promises of God are Yes in Christ. Not a handful, not the easy ones. Every single one, and that's why he says our Amen goes up through Him to the glory of God. That's a whole lot of Yes.
Some would be a smaller Yes than Paul gives. He says all the promises of God are Yes in Christ. Not a select few, not the ones we like best. All of them.

Most sounds pretty generous, and it's still short. Paul says all the promises of God are Yes in Christ. I wouldn't hand out most of a cookie box, and God doesn't hand out most of a promise. The word is all.
True! Paul writes that God “placed His seal on us…” Right next to that, he says God anointed them and put His Spirit in their hearts. It's a list of what God has done, and it's a good list.

Paul does say it. In 2 Corinthians 1:22 he writes that God “placed His seal on us…” It comes right after he says God anointed them. So this one's True, and it's just one piece of what God has done for them.
His Spirit, baker. Paul says God “put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” A pledge is a promise held in advance. So the Spirit in their hearts points ahead to what's coming.

His law is a big word in the Bible, but Paul doesn't use it here. He writes that God “put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” The thing in their hearts is the Spirit. That's the one to hold on to.

His fear isn't what Paul says is placed in the heart here. He writes that God “put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come.” The Spirit is the pledge. A pledge is a promise held in advance, so it's a gift pointing ahead.

To spare the church, baker. Paul calls God as his witness that it was to spare them that he didn't return to Corinth. He takes it that seriously. When a man swears this way, you don't need to read between the lines.

Macedonia is part of Paul's travel plan, but resting there isn't what he says. He calls God as his witness that he didn't return to Corinth to spare them. That's the reason in the text. Anything else would be me guessing, and I try not to guess about Paul.

Judea was where Paul wanted to be sent on his way. But he doesn't give it as the reason he stayed away from Corinth. He says it was to spare them, and he calls God as his witness. That's the reason in the text.

Workers, friend! Paul says they don't lord it over the church's faith. They're fellow workers with the Corinthians for their joy. That puts everybody in the same kitchen, sleeves up. I like a boss who picks up a whisk.

Soldiers sounds tough, but Paul doesn't say it. He says they're fellow workers with the Corinthians for their joy. He's pushing against the idea of lording it over their faith. So the word is workers.

Prisoners is a heavy word, and it's not Paul's word here. He says they're fellow workers with the Corinthians for their joy. That's a team, working together. It's a much better fit for a bakery than a cell.
Painful, baker. Paul says he made up his mind not to make another painful visit. That tells us a painful visit already happened. He's choosing a different way this time.
Short is a reasonable guess, but it's not what the verse says. Paul writes that he decided not to make another painful visit. It wasn't about how long. It was about how much it hurt.
A surprise visit would be a different kind of story. But Paul says he decided not to make another painful visit. The word he uses is about how hard it was. Nothing in the verse mentions a surprise.

Those he grieved, friend. Paul asks, if he grieves the Corinthians, who is left to cheer him but those whom he has grieved? So their joy matters to him. He can't be cheered up from far away by people he's hurt.

Silvanus and Timothy are named earlier in this passage as preaching in Corinth with Paul (2 Corinthians 1:19). But they aren't who he names here. He says the one left to cheer him is those whom he has grieved. That's the Corinthians themselves.

Macedonia shows up earlier in Paul's travel plans, but not in this question. He asks who is left to cheer him but those whom he has grieved. That points to the Corinthians. Not a different church down the road.

True, baker. Paul says he wrote so that on his arrival he would not be grieved by those who ought to make him rejoice. He also says he had confidence in all of them, that they'd share his joy. He's hoping for a good reunion.

Paul says this is true. He writes so that on his arrival he would not be grieved by those who ought to make him rejoice. He also says he had confidence in all of them. So the letter was meant to get things sorted before he showed up.

How much he loves them, baker. Paul says he wrote through many tears out of great distress and anguish of heart, “not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” That's a heavy letter, written by a man who cares. I think it hurt him to write it.

explanations.answer: How angry he is with them
explanations.explanation: Anger isn't what Paul says. He writes that he wrote through many tears, “not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” Tears and anguish don't sound like a man trying to scold. The point is love.
Owing is a different kind of letter. Paul writes that he wrote through many tears, “not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you.” Nothing in the verse mentions a debt. It's all love.
Paul says it the other way around. He says the one who caused grief has not grieved him but all of you, to some degree, not to overstate it. So the church felt it too. It wasn't just Paul's problem.

That's right, friend. Paul says anyone who has caused grief has not grieved him but all of the Corinthians, to some degree, not to overstate it. So the hurt belonged to the whole church. And notice Paul is careful here, not piling it on.
Forgive and comfort him, baker. Paul says, “you ought to forgive and comfort him…” The punishment has been done, and now comes mercy. That's a good turn from a man who has plenty to be sore about.
Distance would be the easy path, but it's not what Paul says. He tells them, “you ought to forgive and comfort him…” The punishment by the majority has been enough. So the next step is forgiveness.
Paul doesn't ask for a trip. He tells the church, “you ought to forgive and comfort him…” The work is for the Corinthians to do, right where they are. Forgiveness and comfort.
Sorrow, friend. Paul says they should forgive and comfort him “so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” So even after punishment, there's a limit. Paul doesn't want him buried.

Pride is a fair thing to worry about in a lot of stories, but it's not in this verse. Paul says to forgive and comfort him “so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” The danger he names is sorrow. So comfort is the fix.
Debt would need an entirely different verse. Paul says to forgive and comfort the man “so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.” Nothing about money anywhere. Just sorrow.

Obedient, baker. Paul says his purpose in writing was to see if they would “stand the test and be obedient in everything.” So the letter had a test in it. And the way he talks, I think he's hoping they pass.

Generous is a lovely quality, but it's not the word here. Paul says his purpose was to see if they would “stand the test and be obedient in everything.” The test is about obedience. That's what he wanted to see.

Patient is a good thing to be, and I could use more of it by the oven. But Paul doesn't use it here. He says his purpose was to see if they would “stand the test and be obedient in everything.” The word is obedient.

Christ, friend. Paul says that if he has forgiven anything, he has forgiven it in the presence of Christ for their sake. So his forgiveness isn't done in secret, and it isn't about him. It's in front of Christ, for the church.
Titus isn't named anywhere in these verses. Paul says he forgave in the presence of Christ for their sake. So forgiveness happens in front of Christ. That's the one to remember.

Silvanus is named earlier in this passage as preaching in Corinth with Paul (2 Corinthians 1:19). But he's not who Paul points to here. Paul says he forgave it in the presence of Christ for their sake. That's the right name.

Satan, baker. Paul says he forgives so that Satan should not outwit them, and adds, “we are not unaware of his schemes.” So forgiveness is part of staying out of Satan's way. It's a serious line, and Paul says it plainly.
Demetrius doesn't appear in these verses. Paul says he forgives so that Satan should not outwit them, and adds, “we are not unaware of his schemes.” The name here is Satan. Keep that one.
Alexander isn't named in this passage. Paul says he forgives so that Satan should not outwit them, and adds, “we are not unaware of his schemes.” That's the one Paul names. Satan.
